evidence.title: Palatine Hill Iron Age Huts & Earliest City Boundary (Rome)
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon on Latial Phase IIB/III Palatine postholes, 8th-century BCE lower-slope tufa wall fills, and Roman annalistic tradition.
evidence.summary: Archaeological transformation of hilltop Tiber sheep-herding villages along the Via Salaria salt ford into drained paved urban Forum Boarium/Forum Romanum under the Roman Kingdom.
evidence.limits: Exact canonical '753 BCE' Romulean foundation date is literary chronology layered atop continuous 9th–8th century BCE huts.

evidence.title: Servian Walls, Republican Census Comitia & Italian Federation (Rome)
evidence.dateBasis: Grotta Oscura tufa blocks Quarried after Veii (378 BCE wall rebuild) plus earliest census-class tribal institutional memory.
evidence.summary: Construction of Rome's 11-kilometer volcanic tufa urban fortification ring paired with property-class census rolls (censors every 5 years, lustrum) organizing citizen tax and legionary levy.
evidence.limits: 6th-century Servius Tullius citizen tallies preserved by Livy are debated by historians; visible ashlar walls date largely to the 378 BCE post-Gallic rebuild.

evidence.title: Conquest of Veii & Latin Settlement Reorganization (Central Italy)
evidence.dateBasis: Historical siege of Etruscan Veii (396 BCE), Latin War settlement (338 BCE), and colonial land centuriation.
evidence.summary: Doubled Rome's ager publicus farmland and pioneered graduated municipium citizenship tiers (full franchise, sine suffragio, allied socii), turning conquered neighbors into military manpower.
evidence.limits: Dates rely on Republican fasti paired with rural field-survey pottery jumps in South Etruria.

evidence.title: Via Appia & Aqua Appia (First Paved Highway & Aqueduct, Rome–Brundisium)
evidence.dateBasis: Censor Appius Claudius Caecus' 312 BCE milestone foundation extending Rome → Capua → Beneventum → Brundisium.
evidence.summary: Engineered Rome's dual template of imperial power: the 16-km subterranean Aqua Appia feeding urban water demand and the flagship volcanic-basalt 'Regina Viarum' military-and-trade highway.
evidence.limits: Basalt polygonal flagstone surfacing largely dates to later Republican/Imperial repavings over gravel agger beds.

evidence.title: Provincialization of Macedonia, Achaea & Africa (Corinth, 146 BCE)
evidence.dateBasis: Historical 146 BCE sack of Corinth & Carthage followed by construction of the trans-Balkan Via Egnatia and Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis.
evidence.summary: Year in which the Roman Republic simultaneously annexed Greece/Macedonia and North Africa—converting Rome into master of the entire Mediterranean sea basin.
evidence.limits: Destruction horizon at Corinth in 146 BCE preceded Julius Caesar's 44 BCE Latin refoundation.

evidence.title: Siege of Alesia & Provincialization of Transalpine Gaul (Burgundy, France)
evidence.dateBasis: Julius Caesar's Commentarii matched precisely to double circumvallation trenches, siege artillery, and mixed Gallic/Germanic coin hoards on Mont-Auxois.
evidence.summary: Climactic 52 BCE encirclement ending Gallic independence and bringing continental Atlantic Gaul—with Lugdunum, Nîmes, and Rhine markets—into Rome's provincial census and road grid.
evidence.limits: Caesarian army sizes remain debated against excavated trench camp capacities.

evidence.title: Battle of Actium & Imperial Wheat Granary of Egypt (Alexandria)
evidence.dateBasis: Naval battle off Ambracian Gulf (31 BCE), Augustus' Alexandria entry (30 BCE), and Cornelius Gallus trilingual tax stele.
evidence.summary: Octavian annexed Ptolemaic Egypt as an imperial personal estate whose massive Nile wheat harvests (~135,000+ tonnes/yr Grain Annona) stabilized urban Rome's million residents for centuries.
evidence.limits: Egyptian prefects excluded senators from entry without imperial leave.

evidence.title: Augustus & Claudius Citizen Censuses (Res Gestae Divi Augusti, Rome)
evidence.dateBasis: Exact epigraphic bronze counts preserved on Ankara/Rome Res Gestae 8 (28 BCE: 4,063,000; 8 BCE: 4,233,000; 14 CE: 4,937,000) and Claudius 47 CE lustrum (5,984,072; Tacitus Annals 11.25).
evidence.summary: Cornerstone demographic anchor of classical antiquity: imperial censors conducted empire-wide property and family registrations; modern historians debate whether totals counted only adult male citizens (~20–25M total citizens + women/children) or all free citizens within a ~50–70M overall Empire.
evidence.limits: Numbers reflect registered Roman citizens; provincial non-citizens (peregrini) and enslaved millions were counted separately in provincial censuses until 212 CE.

population.note: Augustus & Agrippa first Imperial lustrum (28 BCE): 4,063,000 Roman capita civium recorded in Res Gestae 8.
Augustus second census (8 BCE): 4,233,000 Roman citizens registered.
Augustus third census with Tiberius (14 CE): 4,937,000 Roman citizens.
Claudius 47/48 CE imperial lustrum (Tacitus Annals 11.25): 5,984,072 registered Roman citizens.

evidence.title: Quirinius' 6 CE Syrian Census, Apamea Stele & 212 CE Universal Citizenship
evidence.dateBasis: Funerary cursus inscription of Q. Aemilius Secundus (CIL III 6687) registering 117,000 homines cives at Apamea paired with Caracalla's 212 CE Constitutio Antoniniana.
evidence.summary: Rare surviving non-Egyptian provincial tax census record demonstrating how Roman governors counted provincial cities to assess poll-tax (tributum capitis), culminating in 212 CE when Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to virtually every free inhabitant across Europe, North Africa, and West Asia (~55–70M total people).
evidence.limits: Exact imperial population totals remain demographic reconstructions (50–70M consensus bracket) rather than one surviving empire-wide register.

population.note: Municipal/territory census of Apamea Syria (CIL III 6687, 6 CE): 117,000 registered cives/inhabitants under Q. Aemilius Secundus.
Scholarly consensus mid-2nd-century Antonine Roman Empire total population envelope (~55–70 million prior to Antonine Plague impact).

evidence.title: Roman Egyptian 14-Year Census Papyri (Oxyrhynchus & Fayum)
evidence.dateBasis: Over 300 surviving original kat' oikian apographai house-by-house papyrus tax declarations preserved in dry Arsinoite & Oxyrhynchite sands.
evidence.summary: Humanity's most granular ancient census dataset outside Han China: every 14 years heads of household filed sworn lists stating every resident's name, relationship, exact age, occupation, physical scar, and slave status—exposing high infant mortality, life expectancy ~22–25 at birth, and urban vs. village household shapes.
evidence.limits: Dry papyrus survival clusters in Middle Egypt towns and villages, not Delta wetlands.

evidence.title: Vindolanda Roman Frontier Garrison & Ink Wooden Tablets (Northumberland)
evidence.dateBasis: Anaerobically preserved alder/birch leaf writing tablets dated by consular years & cohort strength reports (~97–105 CE).
evidence.summary: World's richest daily-life frontier archive before Hadrian's Wall was built: strength reports of Batavia & Tungrian auxiliary soldiers stationed along the Stanegate road, Claudian birthday party invitations, footwear requisitions, and socks.
evidence.limits: Waterlogged ditch preservation captures ~35 years out of three Roman centuries.

evidence.title: Hadrian's Wall Frontier Barrier & Vallum (Tyne–Solway, Britain)
evidence.dateBasis: Building inscriptions of Legions II, VI, and XX under governor Aulus Platorius Nepos (122–128 CE) through 5th-century sub-Roman continuity.
evidence.summary: 117-kilometer stone-and-turf barrier featuring milecastles every Roman mile, turrets, 16 major auxiliary forts housing soldiers from Syria, Spain, Dacia, and Africa, and the massive southern Vallum earthwork.
evidence.limits: Served as a customs/intelligence perimeter and patrol highway rather than an impenetrable anti-army fortress wall.

evidence.title: Antonine Wall Turf Rampart (Firth of Forth–Clyde, Scotland)
evidence.dateBasis: Twenty ornate sculpted Legionary 'Distance Slabs' (Bridgeness, Balmuildy) measuring exact feet constructed by Emperor Antoninus Pius.
evidence.summary: 63-kilometer timber-and-turf rampart fronted by a deep V-ditch marking the northernmost permanent frontier of the entire Roman Empire across Scotland's central lowlands.
evidence.limits: Occupied briefly (~20 years) before legions withdrew back to Hadrian's Wall in the mid-160s CE.

evidence.title: Upper Germanic–Rhaetian Limes Palisade & Forts (Saalburg–Regensburg)
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology on oak palisade trunks (~119–120 CE Hadrianic line) & abandonment prior to Alamannic Limes Fall ~260 CE.
evidence.summary: 550-kilometer fortified frontier knitting the Middle Rhine to the Upper Danube across >60 forts and 900 watchtowers, marking Europe's longest continuous classical monument.
evidence.limits: Relied on watchtowers and timber/stone walls in open forest terrain rather than river patrols alone.

evidence.title: Carnuntum & the Middle/Lower Danube Limes (Austria–Romania)
evidence.dateBasis: Legionary XV Apollinaris bricks, Marcus Aurelius Meditations composed at Carnuntum (171–175 CE), and Pannonian cavalry road milestones.
evidence.summary: Supreme legionary headquarters guarding the Amber Road Danube crossing near Vienna—evolving from timber-earth camps into a major stone fortress, amphitheater, and civil metropolis.
evidence.limits: Sub-Danubian frontier collapsed into foederati settlement treaties after early 5th c. Hunnic pressures.

evidence.title: Apollodorus' Danube Bridge (Drobeta) & Ulpia Traiana Dacian Road
evidence.dateBasis: 103–105 CE construction inscription of Emperor Trajan + 20 monumental masonry river piers bridging 1,135 m across the Danube.
evidence.summary: World's longest arch bridge for a millennium: Apollodorus of Damascus spanned the lower Danube with 20 ashlar piers and wooden superstructures to supply Roman Dacia's gold mines and imperial highway to Napoca/Porolissum.
evidence.limits: Aurelian evacuated trans-Danubian Dacia in ~271 CE, leaving bridge piers standing on both shores.

evidence.title: Fossatum Africae & Lambaesis Legio III Augusta Base (Algeria)
evidence.dateBasis: Hadrian's famous 128 CE Lambaesis adlocutio military review inscription paired with aerial-photographed Numidian frontier ditches & wall segments.
evidence.summary: 750-kilometer intermittent linear ditch, stone-and-mud wall, and tower network stretching across arid Algerian Aurès foothills—channeling seasonal pastoral transhumance and Sahara caravan traffic through taxable customs gates.
evidence.limits: Built as discontinuous hydraulic-and-customs segments rather than one unbroken wall.

evidence.title: Limes Arabicus, Via Traiana Nova & Qasr Bshir Fort (Jordan)
evidence.dateBasis: Via Nova Traiana 111–114 CE paving milestones ('a finibus Syriae usque ad mare Rubrum') plus 293–305 CE Tetrarchic Latin lintel at Qasr Bshir.
evidence.summary: Trans-Jordan desert defense-in-depth uniting Trajan's paved trunk highway from Syria to Aqaba on the Red Sea with desert quadriburgia castella guarding caravan wells and nomadic pastoral routes.
evidence.limits: Archaeological evidence shows forts facilitated police control and caravan tolls as much as desert warfare.

evidence.title: Dura-Europos Euphrates Garrison, Painted Synagogue & 256 CE Siege
evidence.dateBasis: Latin military papyri of Cohors XX Palmyrenorum and the dramatic 256 CE Sasanian counter-mine collapse freezing armored soldiers and chemical-smoke battle remains.
evidence.summary: Mesopotamian Pompeii on Rome's eastern desert limit: preserving multilingual Greek/Latin/Aramaic/Middle Persian graffiti, the world's oldest surviving house-church, a painted Synagogue, and the earliest archaeological chemical warfare in siege mines.
evidence.limits: Abandoned permanently after Shapur I's 256 CE conquest, freezing mid-3rd century Roman eastern frontier diversity.

evidence.title: Aurelian Walls of Rome (19 km Imperial Defensive Ring)
evidence.dateBasis: Third-century brick-faced concrete fortifications ordered by Emperor Aurelian around Rome's expanded 14 regions.
evidence.summary: Constructed rapidly in five years after 3rd-century Germanic raids reached northern Italy—encircling 1,372 hectares with 381 rectangular bastions and double-tiered artillery galleries still standing around modern Rome.
evidence.limits: Maintained continuously as Rome's primary military perimeter by Ostrogoths, Byzantines, and Popes through 1870 CE.

evidence.title: Triple Theodosian Land Walls & Water Cisterns (Constantinople)
evidence.dateBasis: Praetorian Prefect Anthemius' 408–413 CE triple-layered limestone-and-brick barrier repairing 447 CE earthquake breaches in 60 days.
evidence.summary: History's most formidable pre-modern urban fortification—pairing a 20 m wide moat, inner & outer crenellated curtain walls, and 96 artillery towers that repelled Huns, Avars, Arab fleets, Rus', and Bulgars for over 1,000 years until 7-ton Ottoman super-bombards breached them in 1453.
evidence.limits: Sea walls along Golden Horn and Marmara faced distinct naval siege challenges.

evidence.title: Portus Imperial Hexagonal Basin & Monte Testaccio (Ostia/Rome)
evidence.dateBasis: Claudian sea-basin moles (42–64 CE), Trajan's 33-hectare hexagonal inner basin (106–113 CE), and 53 million discarded Spanish Dressel 20 olive-oil amphorae stacked in Rome.
evidence.summary: Engineered artificial port-and-canal supply machine receiving Egyptian grain ships and Baetican olive-oil fleets that sustained imperial Rome's estimated ~800,000–1,000,000 population.
evidence.limits: Urban Rome peak population estimates vary between ~750k and >1M depending on grain dole multipliers.

evidence.title: Flavian Amphitheatre (Colosseum) & Hadrian's Unreinforced Concrete Pantheon
evidence.dateBasis: Colosseum dedicatory inscription reconstructed over spoils of Judaea (80 CE); Pantheon brick stamps of Trajan/Hadrian (~118–126 CE).
evidence.summary: Twin pinnacles of Roman pozzolanic concrete and brick-arch structural genius—the 43.3-meter unreinforced Pantheon dome utilizing graded pumice/tufa aggregate remains the world's largest unreinforced solid-concrete dome nearly 1,900 years later.
evidence.limits: Monumental Imperial showcase projects fueled by imperial plunder and brickyard monopolies.

evidence.title: Pont du Gard 49 m Three-Tiered Aqueduct Bridge (Nemausus / Nîmes, Gaul)
evidence.dateBasis: Precision-cut dry yellow molasse ashlar blocks up to 6 tonnes spanning 275 m across the Gardon gorge.
evidence.summary: High point of the 50-kilometer Uzès–Nîmes aqueduct maintaining an extraordinary ~34 cm/km average gradient through hills and the 49-meter three-tier arcade to deliver ~35,000 cubic meters of daily spring water.
evidence.limits: Calcium carbonate sinter deposits inside the channel reveal progressive maintenance decay after the 4th–5th century.

evidence.title: Las Médulas Hydraulic Gold Mines & Segovia Granite Aqueduct (Hispania)
evidence.dateBasis: Over 400 km of high-Sierra hydraulic leat canals and Pliny's firsthand description of ruina montium mountainside gold sluicing.
evidence.summary: Ancient world's largest open-cast hydraulic mining landscape: Roman engineers channeled mountain rivers into shafted conglomerate cliffs, detonating entire hills by hydrostatic pressure to wash out ~5,000 kg+ gold bullion yearly powering the Roman denarius-aureus currency.
evidence.limits: Unparalleled environmental transformation leaving dramatic jagged red-clay spire cliffs across León.

evidence.title: Rio Tinto Copper, Silver & Archimedean Screw Waterwheel Mines (Baetica, Spain)
evidence.dateBasis: Greenland ice-core atmospheric lead-pollution spike calibrated to Iberian galena-silver smelting mounds & 40+ wooden drainage waterwheels.
evidence.summary: Deep subterranean industrial mining complex utilizing stacked pairs of 4.5-meter wooden tread-wheels lifting acid mine drainage water 30+ meters vertical—producing coin silver bullion traceable in Arctic ice cores.
evidence.limits: Atmospheric lead anomalies capture Peak Imperial metallurgy followed by Antonine-era decline.

evidence.title: Lugdunum (Lyon): Imperial Mint & Four Aqueducts of the Three Gauls
evidence.dateBasis: Munatius Plancus' 43 BCE colonial foundation charter, Claude's 48 CE Lyon Tablet bronze speech admitting Gallic aristocrats to Rome's Senate, and Gier inverted-siphon aqueduct.
evidence.summary: Administrative hub where the Rhône–Saône rivers joined four pressurized siphon aqueducts, an imperial gold-and-silver coin mint, and Rome's political incorporation of provincial Gallic elites.
evidence.limits: Gier inverted lead siphons required astonishingly complex stone header tanks across deep valleys.

evidence.title: Augusta Treverorum (Trier) & Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium (Rhine Axis)
evidence.dateBasis: Porta Nigra stone gate, Constantinian 310 CE Aula Palatina throne hall, and Cologne 98 km Eifel limestone-canal aqueduct.
evidence.summary: Grew from forward Rhine army supply depots along Agrippa's Gaul road grid into late-imperial Western capital of Constantine and Valentinian I, projecting Mediterranean urbanism deep into northern Europe.
evidence.limits: Late-4th-century imperial court relocation to Milan and Ravenna left Rhine capitals vulnerable to Frankish raids.

evidence.title: Emerita Augusta (Mérida) & Via de la Plata Trunk Highway (Lusitania, Spain)
evidence.dateBasis: Augustus' 25 BCE veteran colony foundation for Legions V Alaudae and X Gemina with 792 m Guadiana granite bridge & Los Milagros aqueduct.
evidence.summary: Model veteran settlement town orchestrating Roman urban planning, granite bridge logistics, Lusitanian road milestones, and Atlantic-to-Interior Spain transport up the Silver Route (Via de la Plata).
evidence.limits: Multi-period Visigothic and Umayyad reoccupation reused Roman monumental marble cores.

evidence.title: Ephesus & Aphrodisias: Province of Asia, Customs Law & Imperial Road Integration
evidence.dateBasis: Lex Portorii Asiae Customs Monument at Ephesus, Sebasteion imperial reliefs, and 614 CE Persian/earthquake urban contraction.
evidence.summary: Richest eastern Mediterranean urban network uniting Asian marble workshops, harbors (continually dredged against Cayster siltation), and imperial post roads linking Rome to Syria.
evidence.limits: Prograding alluvial delta silted Ephesus' Roman harbor completely inland over late antiquity.

evidence.title: Diocletian's Palace (Split), Tetrarchy & Price Edict 301 CE (Dalmatia)
evidence.dateBasis: Epigraphic copies of Diocletian's 301 CE Edict on Maximum Prices (fixing wages & freight tariffs across roads/sea) and Split fortified retirement palace.
evidence.summary: Transformed the Crisis-of-the-Third-Century Empire into a durable Tetrarchy dividing Eastern and Western administrative prefectures—doubling bureaucracy, revamping gold solidus taxation (jugatio-capitatio), and hardening military frontiers.
evidence.limits: Price Edict inscriptions survive mostly in Greek eastern provinces; maximum price caps failed to halt silver coin debasement.

evidence.title: Constantine's Refoundation of Byzantium as Constantinople (324–337 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Imperial dedicatory milestone column (Milion), Hippodrome obelisk foundations, and shifting grain-fleet terminal from Egypt toward the Bosporus.
evidence.summary: Strategic relocation of imperial gravity center to the Bosporus chokepoint linking Europe and Asia—safeguarded between Danube & Euphrates armies, launching Christianized Eastern Roman governance lasting another 1,123 years.
evidence.limits: Western Senate remained in Rome even as decisive imperial coinage and mint control shifted east.

evidence.title: Ravenna Marsh Capital & Dissolution of the Western Roman Court (402–476 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Emperor Honorius' retreat behind Po wetlands & Classis naval port (402 CE); Odoacer's 476 CE deposition of Romulus Augustulus.
evidence.summary: Culmination of 5th-century Western imperial contraction as Britain (410), Africa (439 Vandal loss of grain taxes), Gaul, and Hispania fractured into Germanic successor kingdoms, sending Italy's imperial regalia east to Constantinople.
evidence.limits: Administrative Roman law, Latin literacy, cities, and Senates continued inside Ostrogothic and Frankish realms after 476 CE.

evidence.title: Justinian's Hagia Sophia, Corpus Juris Civilis & Mediterranean Reconquest (527–565 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: 532–537 CE Anthemius & Isidore cathedral construction, Digest/Code codification (534 CE), and Belisarius–Narses recovery of North Africa, Italy, and southern Iberia.
evidence.summary: High-water mark of 6th-century Eastern Roman power—codifying Roman Civil Law for modern Europe, raising Hagia Sophia's floating 31 m pendentive dome, and briefly uniting the Mediterranean rim again right before the 541 CE Justinianic Plague.
evidence.limits: Overspent reconquest armies soon gave way to Lombard Italy, Sasanian wars, and 7th-century Arab conquests.

evidence.title: Byzantine Theme System & Survival of the 674–718 CE Arab Sieges
evidence.dateBasis: Historical chronicle accounts of Greek Fire siphons (c. 674–678 & 717–718 CE), provincial Anatolian Theme seals, and Theodosian Wall defense.
evidence.summary: Pivotal transformation of Late Antique East Rome into the resilient medieval Greek-speaking Christian Empire ('Romaioi'): reorganizing Anatolia into hereditary military Themes and halving Umayyad expansion at the Bosporus.
evidence.limits: Internal political turmoil ended after 717 CE under Leo III, launching Macedonian-era stabilization.

evidence.title: Fall of Constantinople (29 May 1453): End of the 2,206-Year Roman State
evidence.dateBasis: Mehmed II's 53-day artillery siege, Orban's giant bronze siege bombards vs. Gate of St. Romanus Theodosian masonry, and death of Constantine XI Palaiologos.
evidence.summary: Final fall of Rome's direct uninterrupted eastern institutional lineage nearly two millennia after Rome's Republic—propelling Greek manuscript scholars westward across Italy during the Renaissance while turning Istanbul into the Ottoman Imperial seat.
evidence.limits: Small Venetian-held Roman client islands and Trebizond (1461) fell within years of 1453.

waves.title: Via Appia ('Regina Viarum' — Republican Construction Rome–Brundisium)
waves.summary: Rome's prototypical all-weather paved highway begun 312 BCE under Appius Claudius Caecus across the Pontine Marshes to Capua and pushed to Tarentum & Adriatic Brundisium by ~264–241 BCE.
waves.limits: Generalized polyline linking major Republican milestones; upgraded across Imperial centuries.

waves.title: Via Appia & Via Traiana (Imperial Italy–Greece Ferry Trunk Route)
waves.summary: Long-lived Italian arterial carrying magistrates, legions, Ostia/Brundisium grain couriers, and eastern embarkations across Apulia toward Via Egnatia.
waves.limits: Combines original southern Appia alignment and Trajan's 109 CE Beneventum–Bari–Brundisium shortcut.

waves.title: Via Flaminia & Via Aemilia (Rome Across Apennines & Po Valley)
waves.summary: Northern Italian colonizing corridor (Flaminia 220 BCE to Rimini; Aemilia 187 BCE to Piacenza) anchoring Latin colonies, Po agriculture, and trans-Alpine expeditions.
waves.limits: Simplified centerline linking Rome, Spoleto, Rimini, Bologna, Parma, and Piacenza.

waves.title: Via Egnatia (Dyrrhachium–Thessaloniki–Constantinople Overland Highway)
waves.summary: 1,120-kilometer paved continuation of the Via Appia across Adriatic mountains, Lake Ohrid, Thessaloniki, and Thrace to Constantinople—spine of both Roman and Byzantine Balkan administration.
waves.limits: Follows classical Roman–Byzantine milestone alignment reconstructed in Itiner-e (2025).

waves.title: Via Domitia, Via Augusta & Via Agrippa (Italy–Gaul–Hispania Axis)
waves.summary: First Roman highway in Gaul (118 BCE) linked by Augustus down Spain's Mediterranean coast (Via Augusta) to Gades—carrying Baetican silver, olive oil, wines, and Gaulish Samian wares.
waves.limits: Merges Alpine Via Domitia with Pyrenean-to-Cadiz Via Augusta trunk corridor.

waves.title: North African Imperial Coastal & Limes Road (Carthage–Leptis–Alexandria)
waves.summary: Southern Mediterranean Roman coastal corridor knitting Tingis, Caesarea, Carthage, Sabratha/Leptis Magna, Cyrenaica, and Alexandria with inland Numidian granaries.
waves.limits: Schematic coastal trunk line omitting interior Lambaesis and Tripoli oasis branches.

waves.title: Via Militaris (Singidunum / Belgrade–Serdica–Philippopolis–Constantinople)
waves.summary: Diagonal Balkan military artery linking Middle Danube legions through Naissus, Sofia, Plovdiv, and Adrianople straight to the Bosporus—used alike by Roman emperors, Crusaders, and armies.
waves.limits: Connects major Danubian-Thracian cursus publicus relay cities (mansiones).

waves.title: Watling Street & Fosse Way (Dover–London–Chester & Exeter–Lincoln)
waves.summary: Ramrod-straight Claudian-Flavian military and postal arteries uniting Channel ports, Londinium, and York/Hadrian's Wall across Roman Britain.
waves.limits: Traces primary Watling–Stanegate spine; omits secondary cross-diagonal Fosse Way leg.

waves.title: Via Claudia Augusta & Upper Danube–Rhine Military Road
waves.summary: Trans-Alpine paved pass crossing Reschen/Brenner from northern Italy to Augusta Vindelicum (Augsburg) and east along the fortified Danube bank to Carnuntum.
waves.limits: Combines Alpine Via Claudia pass with Rhaetian-Norican Danube border road.

waves.title: Via Traiana Nova & Strata Diocletiana (Damascus–Petra–Red Sea)
waves.summary: Eastern desert trunk highway built upon annexation of Nabataea (106 CE), linking Syria through Bostra, Philadelphia (Amman), Qasr Bshir, and Petra to the Red Sea Indian Ocean port of Aila (Aqaba).
waves.limits: Generalized eastern desert limes spine across modern Syria and Jordan.

waves.title: Upper Germanic–Rhaetian Limes Palisade & Wall Line (Rhine to Danube)
waves.summary: 550-km artificial frontier linking Rheinbrohl on the Rhine to Hienheim/Regensburg on the Danube across timber palisades, ditches, ramparts, and stone walls.
waves.limits: Schematic frontier perimeter connecting excavated UNESCO Limes watchtower sectors.

waves.title: Hadrian's Wall Line (Tyne–Solway Frontier Barrier)
waves.summary: Northern British frontier stone wall, ditch, Vallum, and Military Way controlling movement between Solway Firth and Wallsend on the Tyne.
waves.limits: Linear frontier schematized in three anchor segments.

territories.title: Roman Republic after the Punic & Macedonian Wars (c. 263–132 BCE)
territories.limits: Schematic Republican core encompassing peninsular Italy, Sicily, Sardinia-Corsica, coastal Hispania, Africa (Carthage 146 BCE), and Macedonia/Achaea.

territories.title: Augustan Early Roman Empire: Rhine–Danube–Euphrates Frame (27 BCE–116 CE)
territories.limits: Schematic Principate perimeter linking Spain, Gaul, southern Britain, Rhine–Danube limits, Anatolia, Syria, Egypt, and North African littoral provinces.

territories.title: Roman Empire at Maximum Territorial Reach: Britain to Dacia & Levant (117–270 CE)
territories.limits: Maximum territorial extent including Trajanic Dacia, Arabia Petraea, northern Britain (Antonine/Hadrian walls), North African Fossatum margins, and Upper Euphrates forts (Dura-Europos).

territories.title: Western Roman Empire prior to 476 CE Transformation
territories.limits: Schematic 395 CE Western court division (Italy, Illyricum west, Gaul, Hispania, Britain, and Africa); effective fiscal control contracted sharply after 410–439 CE.

territories.title: Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire Through Constantinople's Fall (395–1453 CE)
territories.limits: Schematic Aegean–Anatolian–Balkan core of the uninterrupted Eastern Roman Empire across its post-7th-century survival span (Justinianic 6th-century peak expanded across Egypt, Syria, and Italy before contracting after 636–1071 CE).

studies.title: Roman Empire: Censuses, Paved Highways, Frontier Walls & Continuity (753 BCE–1453 CE)
studies.summary: Follow Rome end-to-end across 2,206 years—Palatine Iron Age foundations, Republican and Imperial citizen censuses (Res Gestae, Apamea, Egyptian papyri), 12 paved trunk roads and Limes walls across Europe, North Africa, and West Asia, and Eastern Roman continuity to 1453 CE.
